rationale: I'm switching the Welch PSD from mean-averaging to median-averaging across its 2 s segments. The recordings have no artifact rejection, so a few blinks or movement bursts (especially eyes-open) can inflate delta/theta power in the mean and blur the theta/beta signal. The median estimate ignores those transient segments without needing any thresholds, and it doesn't depend on amplitude scale or recording length, which matters for the external datasets.

For each channel and condition, I'm adding the aperiodic (1/f) exponent and offset. They come from a log-log line fit to the total-power-normalized Welch PSD over 2–40 Hz, leaving out the 7–14 Hz alpha peak. Relative band power mixes periodic oscillations with the broadband background slope. The aperiodic exponent is thought to reflect the brain's excitation/inhibition balance and has been linked to ADHD. It may also explain some of the theta/beta-ratio effect. Normalizing by total power first keeps the offset independent of amplitude scale, which matters for the external datasets.

I'm adding one feature per channel, band and condition: how much band power varies over time, measured as the standard deviation of log band power across the 2-s Welch segments. Round 1 suggests that transient high-power segments (movement, blinks, drowsiness swings) carry ADHD signal: median averaging threw them out and the score dropped sharply. This measure captures that non-stationarity directly. Because it uses log power, it doesn't depend on amplitude scale, and it is roughly independent of recording length.

ADHD is linked to unstable vigilance regulation, meaning arousal drifts down over the course of a quiet resting recording. The temporal-variability gain in round 3 fits this. As a new feature, I'm adding the slope of log band power against time (per minute) in each condition, averaged within 5 scalp regions (frontal, central, temporal, parietal, occipital). Averaging by region keeps it to only 50 features. Because the slope uses log power, it doesn't depend on amplitude scale. Using per-minute slopes also makes it comparable across recordings of different lengths.

I'm choosing the L2 strength of the logistic regression by grouped 5-fold inner CV on the training fold, scored by AUROC, over a log grid of C values. Until now C was fixed at 0.1, even though round 3 doubled the feature count to 520 correlated features (26 channels × 5 bands × 2 measures × 2 conditions) with only a few hundred subjects. How much shrinkage is best is a real question about how spread out the signal is across the scalp, so it should be learned without leakage and not guessed.

I'm adding a sixth band, 55–95 Hz, measured the same way as the others: log power relative to total 1–45 Hz power, plus its variability over time. This band mostly picks up scalp-muscle (EMG) activity. Hyperactive or restless subjects should show more muscle tension and more frequent muscle bursts. Round 1 already showed that transient high-power segments carry ADHD signal, and the current 1–45 Hz bands barely see EMG. The band stops short of the 50 Hz and 100 Hz line-noise peaks, and as a log ratio it doesn't depend on amplitude scale.

I'm adding eye-event features from the frontal channels in each condition. Vertical events come from the Fp1/Fp2 mean, horizontal ones from the speed of the F7−F8 signal. For each, I take the rate per minute and the typical amplitude relative to that recording's background. Blink rate is a known dopaminergic marker, and restless eye movements during rest should be more frequent in ADHD. So far the band-power features only pick up this signal indirectly, through delta power variability. Detection uses a robust threshold (median + MAD), so the features don't depend on amplitude scale, and rates are per minute, so they don't depend on recording length.

The biggest gains so far came from behavioural artifacts: power variability, scalp-muscle (EMG) power and eye-event rates. This round adds the matching event rates for gross movement. In each condition I count bursts that hit many channels at once in two bands: slow 0.1–1 Hz drift (head or body movement, electrode shifts) and 55–95 Hz scalp-muscle activity. For each band I take bursts per minute, the fraction of time above threshold and the typical burst size. Restless or hyperactive subjects should have more of these bursts. Detection uses a robust per-channel threshold (median + MAD) on log amplitude in 0.5 s windows, so the features don't depend on amplitude scale, and rates are per minute, so they don't depend on recording length.

This adds slow 0.1–1 Hz eye-movement features from bipolar eye-sensitive derivations: horizontal F7−F8 and vertical Fp-mean minus Cz. For each, I take log power relative to the same derivation's 1–45 Hz power, its variability across 4 s windows, and its episodic excess (90th percentile minus median). These capture gaze wandering and poor fixation in eyes open, and drowsiness-related slow rolling eye movements in eyes closed, a vigilance-instability marker. The current eye features only see fast blinks and saccades above a high threshold, so they miss both. Like the other behavioural features, the new ones are log ratios within a single derivation, so they don't depend on amplitude scale or reference, and per-window statistics keep them independent of recording length.

I'm adding per-channel slow-drift features for 0.1–1 Hz, which no current feature measures per channel. For each channel I take log RMS relative to that channel's own 1–45 Hz RMS, plus how much that ratio varies across 4 s windows. Round 9's two eye derivations gave the biggest gain so far, but the spectral bands start at 1 Hz. So the topography of slow activity (frontal eye drift, posterior and temporal head or body movement, sweat or electrode drift) and its episodic changes are still unseen. Both measures are ratios within a single channel, so amplitude scale cancels, and per-window statistics keep them independent of recording length.

I'm adding a new per-channel ultra-slow (0.02–0.1 Hz) power feature in each condition. It is log power relative to the channel's own 1–45 Hz power, taken from a Hann-tapered periodogram of the whole recording. The 0.1–1 Hz drift features gave the two largest gains so far, but nothing yet measures slower activity. Slow skin-potential/sweat drifts (sympathetic arousal), slow posture shifts and electrode creep live at 10–50 s periods, and their topography should differ in restless or hyperaroused ADHD subjects. The feature is a ratio within a single channel, so amplitude scale and reference cancel. A fixed frequency band summed from a normalized periodogram also keeps it independent of recording length.

Slow 0.1–1 Hz drift gave the two biggest gains so far (rounds 9 and 10), but each channel was measured on its own. Head or body movement produces drift that rises and falls together across the scalp; sweat and electrode drift are local, and eye movements form a frontal dipole. This change adds how strongly the drift is coordinated across the scalp: each channel's mean correlation with the other channels, plus the share of variance in the first two components of the correlation matrix. These are correlations, so they don't depend on amplitude scale, and they use the whole recording, so length doesn't matter.

The slow-drift coupling in round 12 helped by separating scalp-wide movement from local drift. This change does the same for scalp muscle activity: I'm adding the cross-channel correlation of 55–95 Hz EMG log-RMS envelopes in 0.5 s windows, giving each channel's mean envelope correlation plus the variance share of the two leading eigenvalues. Muscle bursts that rise and fall together across the scalp suggest restless whole-head movement, while local temporal or frontal bursts suggest jaw or forehead tension. The current EMG features only measure power per channel and scalp-wide burst counts. Because these are correlations of log envelopes, they don't depend on amplitude scale or recording length.

I'm adding features that describe how eye events are spread over time, measured on the blinks and saccades that are already detected. For each one I add its typical duration (log half-height width). For each derivation I add how irregular the gaps between events are (standard deviation of log inter-event intervals). Longer blinks are an established marker of drowsiness and low vigilance. Clustered, bursty blinking and saccades are a behavioural sign of restlessness, which the current features don't capture because they only measure rate and amplitude. Both new measures are in seconds or log-interval units, so they don't depend on amplitude scale and are largely independent of recording length.

I'm adding a time-resolved version of the slow-drift (0.1–1 Hz) coupling. Over 10 s windows (50% overlap), I compute the share of variance in the leading eigenvalue of the inter-channel drift correlation matrix. From those per-window shares I take the median, std, 90th percentile and the fraction of windows above 0.5. Round 12's coupling is a single average over the whole recording, so it mixes brief movement episodes with background drift. The per-window shares should show how often and how strongly scalp-wide movement episodes happen, which I expect in restless subjects. Correlations don't depend on amplitude scale, and fractions and percentiles over windows don't depend on recording length. I haven't run this version, so I don't have a score for it yet.

Breathing shows up as a slow, scalp-wide drift that rises and falls with each breath. Breathing rate and how regular it is are markers of arousal and restlessness, and nothing in the current features measures them. This change takes the leading spatial component of the correlation-normalized 0.1–1 Hz drift. From its Welch spectrum (30 s segments) it adds four features: the peak frequency in the breathing range (0.12–0.6 Hz), how much the peak stands out, how much power sits near the peak, and how flat the slow spectrum is (normalized spectral entropy). All four are frequencies or ratios of a normalized signal, so they don't depend on amplitude scale or recording length.

This round adds a heart-rate marker. Heartbeats leak into scalp EEG as periodic QRS spikes in the 15–40 Hz envelope, and heart rate and its regularity reflect autonomic arousal, which differs in ADHD (and stimulant treatment raises it). Breathing features helped last round, but nothing yet measures the heart. I estimate the cardiac peak in the 0.75–2.2 Hz spectrum of each channel's log 15–40 Hz envelope (log ratio to its median, normalized per channel, averaged over channels). The three features are peak frequency, peak prominence and power concentration, and none depends on amplitude scale, reference or recording length. I haven't run this, so there is no Dev score yet.

This adds EEG vigilance-state dynamics, which no current feature measures. ADHD is thought to involve unstable arousal regulation (Hegerl's vigilance model), and the behavioural-artifact gains point the same way. In every 2 s spectrogram segment I compute the posterior alpha-to-(delta+theta) log ratio, a scale-free index of alert alpha versus drowsy slowing, then smooth it with a 3-segment median. From that time series I take five features: the fraction of alpha-dominant segments, the median and 10th percentile of the ratio, its 10–90 percentile spread, and the number of switches between alpha and non-alpha states per minute. The fraction, percentiles and per-minute switch rate don't depend on recording length. This version has not been run, so there is no Dev score for it yet.

I'm adding a measure of electrode-contact instability. Restless head and body movement and sweating change electrode impedance, so the amount of mains noise picked up rises and falls over time. For each channel and condition, I take the line-noise peak (50 or 60 Hz, chosen from the data) in each 2 s spectrogram segment, as a log ratio to its neighbouring 46–54 Hz power so muscle activity cancels out, and then take its standard deviation over segments. I also add one scalp-median level of that ratio. These are within-channel log ratios, so they don't depend on amplitude scale or reference, and the per-segment statistics don't depend on recording length. This version has not been run, so it has no Dev score yet.

Electrode-contact instability (round 19) and scalp-wide movement bursts both helped, but nothing yet catches single-channel transients. When a fidgeting subject touches their head or electrodes shift, single electrodes "pop" with sudden step or spike transients. This change adds, per channel and condition, the per-minute rate of steep derivative transients that are local to that channel (robust-z above the scalp-wide median), plus their scalp-median rate. These are behavioural and contact markers of restlessness, and because they use MAD-normalized rates per minute they don't depend on amplitude scale, reference or recording length.
